1. What medical cannabis is: prescribed context

In the UK, cannabis-based products for medicinal use can be prescribed by a specialist doctor on the GMC specialist register, mostly through private clinics. A prescription is a clinical decision for an individual, with its own monitoring, legal and driving considerations. Nothing on this page replaces that.

2. Flower vs oil, and why dry-herb vaporising can be easier
Flower and oil can feel very different in onset, duration and controllability
. The personal preference here is flower via dry-herb vaporiser
: no rolling, easier with shaky hands or executive dysfunction, no combustion, a more controllable routine, and more consistent supply than informal sources.
Vaporisers heat flower below combustion. Different compounds evaporate at different temperatures, so temperature can change what is inhaled
. Specific temperature targeting for specific effects is part of the personal working notes, not general advice.
Main intoxicating cannabinoid; CB1 receptor agonist
. Licensed THC:CBD spray is used for MS spasticity
Non-intoxicating; licensed for some childhood epilepsies
. May soften some THC effects such as anxiety
Behaves differently from THC at CB1 depending on dose
. A clearer, more functional personal response to THCV-associated cultivars is an N=1 observation
Precursor cannabinoid; α2-adrenergic and other activity in lab studies
Forms as THC ages; weaker at CB1
. Widely marketed for sleep with limited human evidence
Non-intoxicating; anti-inflammatory and TRP-channel activity mainly in preclinical work
Terpenes shape aroma and may contribute to effect. Only β-caryophyllene has well-documented direct cannabinoid-receptor (CB2) binding
. Most other terpene effect claims come from animal or lab studies at doses that may not match inhaled amounts
Earthy, mango. Linked to sedation and muscle relaxation in animal work
Citrus. Anxiolytic signals in small studies
Floral, lavender. Calming effects in animal and aromatherapy studies
Pine. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition in lab work
Humulene: woody, anti-inflammatory in lab work
. Terpinolene-dominant profiles were a poor personal fit
The “entourage effect” is the idea that cannabinoids and terpenes change each other’s effects. It is plausible and widely discussed, but human evidence is still limited

. The MJB notes include a personal mechanistic model linking terpene combinations to motor, attention and arousal effects, including a model framed around SPG7 and ADHD. That model is a personal working hypothesis
Cannabinoids can interact with other medicines through liver enzymes
. Tell the prescriber about every medicine and supplement.
Strain names are marketing labels; measured cannabinoid and terpene composition matters more where it is available. Reviews keep personal experience and product data in separate boxes.

Responses are logged in a living N=1 register: product, batch, time, setting, and the functional result (starting tasks, motor tension, pain, sleep, mood). One person’s log can generate good questions. It cannot establish what works for anyone else
. The register and framework are in the Drive resources below.

An interactive lineage explorer traces which cultivars descend from which. Shared ancestry can suggest similar chemistry, but batch testing beats family assumptions. The explorer is in the cannabis research folder below.
Cannabis can worsen anxiety, cognition, motivation, mood or psychosis risk in some people.
Driving with THC in the body above legal limits is an offence in the UK, including with a prescription if you are impaired.
Long-term evidence for cannabis in ADHD is limited. Most claims here are lived experience or early science.
The personal protocol in the source notes is a working record, not a dosing guide.

The full cannabis source corpus — pharmacology guide, pedigree explorer, chemovar-matching specification, functional-analysis framework, live response register and review template — is held on Google Drive and added to over time.
